specPoints.text: know that magnetism is induced in some materials when they are placed in a magnetic field

primer.text: Permanent magnets keep their poles for decades; induced magnets borrow them for as long as the field lasts. This note sorts the magnetic family — iron, steel, cobalt, nickel — into hard keepers and soft losers, and shows why a magnet plus an unmagnetised material can only ever attract.

lessons.title: Magnetic materials and the permanent/induced split
lessons.opening: Only a short list of substances — iron, steel, cobalt, nickel — respond to magnets at all. Permanent magnets hold their magnetism indefinitely; induced magnets are ordinary magnetic materials that gain poles only while sitting in a field, and always pull towards whatever induced them.
keyPoints: Magnetic materials include iron, steel, cobalt, nickel and alloys containing them.
Non-magnetic materials such as copper, aluminium, plastic and glass are unaffected by magnetic fields.
A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field continuously.
An induced magnet is a magnetic material that becomes magnetised only while in another magnet's field.
The force between a magnet and an induced magnet is always attraction.

low.restatement: A fridge magnet works forever — it is permanent. A paperclip only sticks while it is near the magnet — it is an induced magnet, gaining and losing its pull with the field.
low.analogy: A permanent magnet is a lamp with its own battery; an induced magnet is a reflective panel that shines only while the lamp is on.
low.examPointer: Use the phrase 'while placed in the magnetic field' for induced magnetism — the timing condition is the mark.

medium.restatement: The distinction is persistence of domain alignment: permanent (hard) materials lock their aligned domains, sustaining a field with no external help; induced (soft) materials align only under the applied field and randomise when it leaves. Induction always yields attraction because the alignment places the unlike pole nearest the inducing pole.
medium.analogy: A permanent magnet is a marching band that keeps formation after the music stops; an induced magnet is the band that snaps into step only while the drum plays.
medium.examPointer: For the 'always attraction' claim, justify it geometrically: induced pole nearest the magnet is always unlike, and unlike poles attract.

options.explanation: Aluminium is not a magnetic substance.
Steel is magnetic — it can be induced.
Iron is the classic magnetic element.
Nickel is one of the magnetic elements.

options.text: a magnetic material magnetised while in another magnet's field
options.explanation: Induction is field-driven, temporary magnetisation.

options.text: a magnet that keeps its field for years
options.explanation: That describes a permanent magnet.

options.text: a non-magnetic material pulled by a magnet
options.explanation: Non-magnetic materials are never pulled.

options.text: a magnet made in a factory
options.explanation: Manufacture is irrelevant; the field-driven mechanism defines induction.

check.stem: The force between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet is always:

options.explanation: Induction puts an unlike pole nearest, so the pair attracts.
Repulsion needs two independent magnets with like poles facing.
Induction exists precisely to produce the pull.
The force weakens with distance but stays attractive.

check.stem: A paperclip sticks to a magnet. The magnet is removed and the clip no longer holds a second clip. What type of magnetic material is the clip?

options.explanation: Losing magnetism as soon as the field goes is soft behaviour.
A hard material would keep the induced magnetism.
It was attracted, so it is a magnetic substance.
A permanent clip would keep holding the second one.

check.stem: Which set lists ONLY permanent-magnet behaviour?

options.text: keeps its field with no external help; can repel another magnet
options.explanation: Sustained field plus pole interaction are permanent traits.

options.text: gains poles only near a magnet; loses them when removed
options.explanation: That is induced behaviour.

options.text: attracted to either pole; never repels
options.explanation: Attraction-only describes induced magnets or raw magnetic materials.
Hard permanent magnets resist casual demagnetising.

check.stem: Name four magnetic elements or their alloys.
check.modelAnswer: Iron, steel, cobalt and nickel — steel being the iron alloy used for permanent magnets.

check.stem: State what is always true about the force between a magnet and an unmagnetised magnetic material.
check.modelAnswer: The force is always attraction, whatever pole of the magnet is presented.

check.stem: Explain why an induced magnet always attracts the magnet that induces it.
check.modelAnswer: The field aligns the material's domains so an induced pole forms at its near face that is unlike the facing pole of the magnet. Unlike poles attract, so the interaction is a pull no matter which pole was presented — the geometry of induction guarantees attraction.

check.stem: A technician sorts scrap with a magnet: some pieces stick and stay stuck after release; others fall straight off. Sort the pieces by magnetic class and name each class.
check.modelAnswer: Pieces that stay magnetised after release are made of magnetically hard material and behave as permanent magnets. Pieces that fall straight off were induced magnets of soft magnetic material — they held poles only while in the field.

lessons.title: Permanent magnets at work, inducing and losing magnetism
lessons.opening: Permanent magnets are engineered to forget nothing: hard steels keep their aligned domains for decades. Induced magnets do the opposite — poles appear the moment a field arrives, with the unlike pole always facing the source, and vanish the moment it leaves.
keyPoints: Permanent magnets are made from magnetically hard materials such as steel.
A permanent magnet keeps its field without any external magnet nearby.
Induced magnetism appears only while the material sits in the magnetic field.
The induced pole nearest the inducing magnet is always unlike that pole.
Removing the field — or the magnet — lets an induced magnet lose its magnetism.

low.restatement: A steel fridge magnet never switches off. An iron tack held near it grows a south pole on the side facing the magnet's north pole — and loses it again when taken away.
low.analogy: Permanent magnetism is a tattoo; induced magnetism is a stamp that fades as soon as the stamp is lifted.
low.examPointer: Name the induced pole explicitly in diagram questions: near a north pole, the near face becomes south.

medium.restatement: Induction is domain alignment under an external field: the nearest-face domains flip to present the unlike pole, minimising the system's field energy, which is why the resulting force is attraction. Hard materials resist realignment both ways — that is why they hold permanent magnetism but are slow to induce; soft materials flip freely in both directions.
medium.analogy: Soft material is a crowd that instantly faces whoever shouts; hard material is a crowd that turns slowly but then refuses to turn back.
medium.examPointer: Chain questions: each newly induced clip induces the next — say 'each clip acts as the inducing magnet for the next' for the evaluation mark.

check.stem: Which material suits a PERMANENT magnet?

options.explanation: Hard materials retain their aligned domains permanently.
Soft iron sheds its magnetism when the field leaves.
Copper is non-magnetic.
Plastics carry no magnetic response.

check.stem: A north pole is held near one end of an iron bar. What pole appears at that near end?

options.explanation: Induction always puts the unlike pole nearest.
A near north pole would repel — induction instead attracts.
The field induces poles in the bar.

options.text: both poles at the same end
options.explanation: One face carries one induced pole.

check.stem: When the magnet is taken away from the iron bar, the bar:

options.text: loses most of its induced magnetism
options.explanation: Induced magnetism persists only while the field is present.

options.text: keeps its full induced magnetism forever
options.explanation: Permanent retention is hard-material behaviour; the bar is soft iron.
Nothing reverses; the induced poles simply fade.
It can be induced again at any time.

check.stem: Which observation shows a bar is a PERMANENT magnet rather than an induced one?

options.text: it still attracts pins an hour after being far from any other magnet
options.explanation: Field-free retention is the permanent signature.
Both permanent and induced magnets attract.
Material alone does not settle the magnetisation state.

options.text: it hangs pointing north-south when freely suspended
options.explanation: Earth's field induces that alignment even in soft materials.

check.stem: Steel is described as magnetically HARD. What does 'hard' mean here?

options.text: it keeps its magnetism and resists demagnetising
options.explanation: Hardness refers to retention, not physical scratch resistance.

options.text: it is difficult to cut or drill
options.explanation: Mechanical hardness is not the magnetic meaning.

options.text: it feels hard to the touch
options.explanation: Texture is irrelevant to the magnetic class.
Heating is not part of the hard/soft definition.

check.stem: State what a permanent magnet does that an induced magnet cannot.
check.modelAnswer: A permanent magnet keeps its magnetic field without any external field present.

check.stem: State the pole that appears on the near face of an iron bar next to a south pole.
check.modelAnswer: A north pole is induced on the near face, unlike the facing south pole.

check.stem: Explain why the paperclip chain collapses the instant the top magnet is lifted away.
check.modelAnswer: Every clip in the chain held only induced magnetism, created by the field of the magnet and of the clips above it. Lifting the magnet removes the top field, so the first clip loses its poles and drops; losing it removes the field for the second, and the collapse cascades down the chain.

check.stem: A magnetic door catch must hold the door firmly whenever it is near the frame plate but must never interfere when the door is open. Design the catch's magnetic pairing and justify it.
check.modelAnswer: Fix a small permanent magnet in the frame and fit a soft iron plate on the door. Whenever the door nears the frame the plate becomes an induced magnet and is attracted firmly to the permanent magnet, latching the door; with the door open the plate holds no magnetism, so it does nothing until it is close again.

glossary.definition: A magnet made of hard magnetic material that keeps its field without external help.
A substance, such as iron, steel, cobalt or nickel, that a magnet can attract or induce.
The lining-up of tiny magnetic regions inside a material that gives it net magnetism.

workedExample.prompt: The diagram shows a magnet held close to a piece of metal that is suspended by a light cotton thread. The piece of metal is attracted towards the magnet. Explain this observation, and state what it does and does not prove about the metal.
steps: The magnet's field acts on the suspended metal, so magnetism is induced in it while the field is present.
Induction always places an unlike induced pole nearest the magnet, so the force between them is attraction.
The observation proves the metal is a magnetic substance; it does not prove the metal was already a magnet, because either pole of the magnet would attract it.
A certain test would be to check for repulsion with the magnet's pole — only a true magnet can repel.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The metal is attracted because magnetism is induced in it by the magnet's field; this shows it is a magnetic material but does not show it was magnetised beforehand.
